## Chapter Summary

Internal and external auditors differ in purpose but rely increasingly on the same analytics, which let them test every record in a population instead of a sample. Testing a whole population produces exceptions, most of them false positives, so the auditor's judgment goes into designing each test, investigating each exception, and recording a disposition for it. The work follows a workflow: state the objective, reconcile the population to the ledger, run the tests, investigate the exceptions, record their dispositions, and document the whole in a workpaper.

Reconciling a population's count and total to the general ledger confirms that a test covers every record. Stratification then shows where the value lies: at Charles River, most supplier payments are small, fewer than a thousand payments of $10,000 or more hold about a third of the value, and four payments are large enough to examine one by one. A first-digit test compares the payments' leading digits with Benford's Law, and the mean absolute deviation measures how closely they conform. The payments conform only marginally, and splitting them shows why: partial payments of invoices of $1,000 or more do not conform, because they are a subset selected by size, while full payments and the invoices themselves conform. A nonconforming digit test points to where to look; it does not show that anything is wrong.

An aging schedule classifies open invoices by days past due at an as-of date and supports the estimate of the allowance for credit losses, which the credit loss standard of the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) requires even when the risk of loss is remote. Charles River's customers pay mostly on time, but the reconciliation of the aged invoices to the accounts receivable account found a round difference: an opening balance, recorded in the first journal entry, that no invoice supports and no receipt has reduced. The company has also never recorded an allowance.

Journal entry testing looks for the characteristics that auditing standards associate with fraudulent entries, such as entries recorded after the period they affect, entries by people who do not usually make them, and round amounts, together with tests of approval. Flags for each characteristic add up to a risk score that ranks entries for review. Some flagged patterns have ordinary explanations, such as month-end depreciation on a weekend, while others, such as entries approved by their own creators, point to weaknesses in the approval controls. The highest-scoring entry was the opening balance entry, the same entry that the receivables reconciliation had found. Duplicate, near-duplicate, gap, and threshold tests complete the auditor's toolkit, and a workpaper that records the population, parameters, exceptions, dispositions, and conclusion of each test makes the analytics reviewable and repeatable.
